theory.overview: Pipelining is the architectural technique that transformed processors from lumbering giants into the high-speed engines of modern computing. By overlapping the execution of multiple instructions—similar to how an assembly line manufactures cars—pipelining achieves throughput nearly equal to one instruction per clock cycle, even though each individual instruction still takes several cycles to complete. However, this performance comes with complexity: hazards, stalls, and flushes challenge designers to maintain the pipeline's smooth flow. Understanding pipelining reveals both the art and science of processor design.

sections.title: The Pipeline Concept
sections.content: A non-pipelined processor waits for one instruction to complete before starting the next. A pipelined processor starts a new instruction each cycle while previous instructions continue through subsequent stages. Like a car assembly line where multiple cars are simultaneously being welded, painted, and assembled, a 5-stage pipeline has 5 instructions in various stages of completion. Ideally, CPI (cycles per instruction) approaches 1, though hazards prevent reaching this theoretical maximum.

sections.title: The Classic 5-Stage Pipeline
sections.content: The canonical RISC pipeline consists of 5 stages: IF (Instruction Fetch) reads from memory using PC; ID (Instruction Decode) extracts opcode/operands and reads registers; EX (Execute) performs ALU operations and calculates addresses; MEM (Memory) accesses data memory for loads/stores; WB (Writeback) stores results to registers. Each stage takes approximately equal time, determining the clock period.

sections.title: Data Hazards: Dependencies Stall
sections.content: When an instruction needs a result that a previous instruction hasn't yet produced, we have a data hazard. Read-After-Write (RAW) is the most common—the consumer tries to read before the producer writes back. Solutions include: stalling (inserting bubbles), forwarding/bypassing (sending result directly from EX/MEM to next instruction's EX), and compiler scheduling (reordering instructions to separate dependencies).

hazardTypes.RAW: Read After Write - most common, must wait for result
hazardTypes.WAR: Write After Read - rare in simple pipelines
hazardTypes.WAW: Write After Write - rare in simple pipelines

sections.title: Control Hazards: Branches Disrupt
sections.content: Branch instructions change the PC, but the pipeline doesn't know the target until the Execute stage (or later). By then, subsequent instructions have already been fetched—the wrong ones if the branch is taken! Solutions include: stalling until branch resolves (slow), predicting not-taken (assume fall-through), predicting taken (assume branch goes), delayed branches (execute instructions after branch regardless), and branch prediction with speculative execution.

sections.title: Structural Hazards: Resource Conflicts
sections.content: When two instructions need the same hardware unit simultaneously, a structural hazard occurs. For example, if instruction and data share a single memory (von Neumann), a load/store conflicts with instruction fetch. Solutions include: stalling one instruction, or duplicating resources (Harvard architecture with separate instruction/data memories/caches). Modern CPUs eliminate most structural hazards through resource replication.
examples: Single memory for instructions and data

sections.title: Forwarding: Smart Bypass
sections.content: Forwarding (bypassing) sends a result directly from one pipeline stage to another, avoiding the need to wait for writeback. If instruction 1 computes a result in EX, instruction 2 can receive it at the start of its EX stage (bypassing MEM and WB). This eliminates most RAW stalls. Modern pipelines have extensive bypass networks connecting ALU outputs directly to ALU inputs.
paths: Multiple forwarding muxes at each stage

keyConcepts.name: CPI (Cycles Per Instruction)
keyConcepts.description: Average clock cycles to complete one instruction. Ideal pipeline: CPI = 1.

keyConcepts.name: Pipeline Register
keyConcepts.description: Register between stages holding intermediate results. IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB.

keyConcepts.name: Bubble
keyConcepts.description: A pipeline stall where no work is done—like a NOP inserted to resolve a hazard.

keyConcepts.name: Branch Penalty
keyConcepts.description: Cycles lost when a branch misprediction flushes the pipeline.

steps.title: Fetch First Instruction
steps.description: Start fetching the first instruction into IF stage.

steps.title: Advance and Fetch Second
steps.description: First instruction moves to ID, second enters IF.

steps.title: Fill the Pipeline
steps.description: Continue until all stages are occupied.

steps.title: Handle Dependencies
steps.description: Detect hazards and apply forwarding or stall.

practiceProblems.title: Pipeline Throughput
practiceProblems.description: With a filled pipeline, how many cycles between completing consecutive instructions?
practiceProblems.explanation: In a filled pipeline, one instruction completes every cycle. The latency is 5 cycles, but throughput is 1 instruction per cycle.

practiceProblems.title: RAW Hazard
practiceProblems.description: What type of hazard occurs when an instruction needs a result before it's written back?
practiceProblems.explanation: RAW (Read After Write) is when a later instruction tries to read a value before an earlier instruction writes it. Most common data hazard.

practiceProblems.title: Forwarding Benefit
practiceProblems.explanation: Forwarding sends results directly from ALU to next instruction's ALU, avoiding the need to wait for register writeback. This eliminates most RAW stalls.

practiceProblems.title: Branch Penalty
practiceProblems.description: If a branch resolves in EX stage and is taken, how many fetched instructions must be flushed in a 5-stage pipeline?
practiceProblems.explanation: Instructions in IF and ID stages after the branch are wrong and must be flushed. The branch instruction itself is in EX.
hints: IF and ID have wrong instructions

practiceProblems.title: Pipeline Registers
practiceProblems.description: What passes data between pipeline stages?
practiceProblems.explanation: Pipeline registers (latches) hold intermediate results between stages. They separate timing domains and propagate data forward.

practiceProblems.title: CPI with Stalls
practiceProblems.description: If 20% of instructions cause a 1-cycle stall and branches (20% of instructions) have 2-cycle misprediction penalty with 90% accuracy, what's the effective CPI?

minigame.title: Pipeline Panic
minigame.description: Keep the pipeline flowing at maximum speed! Route instructions through stages, resolve hazards with forwarding or stalls, and minimize bubbles. The smoothest pipeline wins!
instructions: Instructions flow from left (IF) to right (WB) through pipeline stages
Drag results forward to enable forwarding (green arrows)
Click hazard indicators to insert bubbles when forwarding won't work
Branches cause flushes - quickly refill the pipeline!
Keep CPI as close to 1.0 as possible!

snippets.title: Pipeline Simulator
snippets.code:
class PipelineStage:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.instruction = None
        self.data = {}
    
    def accept(self, instruction, data):
        self.instruction = instruction
        self.data = data
    
    def clear(self):
        self.instruction = None
        self.data = {}

class PipelinedCPU:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stages = {
            'IF': PipelineStage('IF'),
            'ID': PipelineStage('ID'),
            'EX': PipelineStage('EX'),
            'MEM': PipelineStage('MEM'),
            'WB': PipelineStage('WB')
        }
        self.pc = 0
        self.cycle = 0
        self.completed = 0
        self.stalls = 0
        self.forwarding_enabled = True
    
    def check_hazard(self, current, next_stage):
        # Simplified RAW hazard detection
        if not current.instruction or not next_stage.instruction:
            return False
        
        # If destination of next equals source of current, hazard
        curr_dest = current.data.get('dest')
        next_srcs = next_stage.data.get('srcs', [])
        
        if curr_dest in next_srcs:
            # Can we forward?
            if self.forwarding_enabled and current.name in ['EX', 'MEM']:
                return 'forward'  # Can forward
            return 'stall'  # Must stall
        return False
    
    def step(self, new_instruction):
        self.cycle += 1
        
        # Check hazards and handle
        hazard = self.check_hazard(self.stages['EX'], self.stages['ID'])
        
        if hazard == 'stall':
            # Insert bubble - don't advance ID to EX
            self.stalls += 1
            # Move WB→done, MEM→WB, EX→MEM, ID stays, IF→ID
            self.stages['WB'].clear()
            self.stages['WB'].accept(self.stages['MEM'].instruction, self.stages['MEM'].data)
            self.stages['MEM'].accept(self.stages['EX'].instruction, self.stages['EX'].data)
            self.stages['EX'].clear()  # Bubble inserted
            # ID stays in place, IF→ID
            self.stages['ID'].accept(self.stages['IF'].instruction, self.stages['IF'].data)
            self.stages['IF'].accept(new_instruction, {'pc': self.pc})
            self.pc += 1
        else:
            # Normal advance
            if self.stages['WB'].instruction:
                self.completed += 1
            
            self.stages['WB'].accept(self.stages['MEM'].instruction, self.stages['MEM'].data)
            self.stages['MEM'].accept(self.stages['EX'].instruction, self.stages['EX'].data)
            self.stages['EX'].accept(self.stages['ID'].instruction, self.stages['ID'].data)
            self.stages['ID'].accept(self.stages['IF'].instruction, self.stages['IF'].data)
            self.stages['IF'].accept(new_instruction, {'pc': self.pc, 'dest': None, 'srcs': []})
            self.pc += 1
    
    def get_cpi(self):
        if self.completed == 0:
            return float('inf')
        return self.cycle / self.completed

    def status(self):
        print(f'Cycle {self.cycle}: CPI={self.get_cpi():.2f}')
        for name in ['IF', 'ID', 'EX', 'MEM', 'WB']:
            instr = self.stages[name].instruction or '---'
            print(f'  {name}: {instr}')

# Test
cpu = PipelinedCPU()
program = ['ADD', 'SUB', 'LOAD', 'STORE', 'ADD', 'MUL', 'DIV', 'ADD']

for i, instr in enumerate(program):
    cpu.step(instr)
    cpu.status()
    print()

print(f'Final CPI: {cpu.get_cpi():.2f}')
